stemBlocks.value: The quantities distance, displacement, speed, velocity, time and acceleration are used to describe the motion of a car. (a) State the THREE vector quantities. (b) State ONE feature that distinguishes a vector from a scalar.
Think first: Ask of each quantity: does it need a direction to make sense?

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p178-q01 from workbook page 178.

contentBlocks.value: Distance, speed and time answer only 'how much'; displacement, velocity and acceleration all need 'in which direction'

solutionSteps.instruction: Name the remaining quantities as scalars.

contentBlocks.value: Distance, speed and time have size only
A vector has both magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only

strategyBlocks.value: Test each quantity for whether a direction is part of its meaning, then state the defining difference.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) The three vector quantities are displacement, velocity and acceleration  (b) A vector has both magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has magnitude only

whyThisWorks.value: The distinction is not about the numbers involved but about what the quantity describes. A speed of 60 km/h tells you nothing about where the car is heading; a velocity of 60 km/h due north does. Because vectors carry direction, they combine by the triangle or parallelogram law rather than by plain addition — which is why 3 km east then 4 km north gives a displacement of 5 km, not 7 km.

commonErrors.misconception: Calling distance a vector by confusing it with displacement.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Calling distance a vector by confusing it with displacement.

commonErrors.misconception: Listing speed as a vector because it has a numerical size.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Listing speed as a vector because it has a numerical size.

commonErrors.misconception: Answering part b with 'a vector is bigger' or 'a vector is an arrow' rather than naming magnitude and direction.

examTip.value: Pair each scalar with its vector partner — distance/displacement, speed/velocity — and the classification questions answer themselves.
